facts.fact: The IGC study says the revenue management systems in Blantyre, Lilongwe and Mzuzu consolidated scattered Excel and Word registers of property and business owners, with their payments and liabilities, into one database per city, used to produce demand notices and business licences.

The IGC study says Zomba's revenue management system, installed in 2017 with about 15 POS devices, covers market rates, bus depots and parking only, not city rates or business licences, and that the POS use lapsed from 2019 and was only slowly reinstated from 2021.

The IGC study says each of the four city councils runs its own cloud-hosted revenue system from a different vendor, with no national push or coordination, and that planned integration with the IFMIS, banks and mobile money had not been achieved in any of the four cities, so receipts were uploaded separately to both systems.

The IGC study says revenue management systems were introduced in all four of Malawi's city councils (Blantyre, Lilongwe, Mzuzu, Zomba) since 2017, out of 35 local governments (28 districts, 4 cities, 3 municipal councils); it names none in the other 31.

The IGC study says the city systems are supplied under revenue-share contracts: Blantyre build-transfer-operate by Technobrain for 7 years at 15-20% of the relevant revenue, Lilongwe by Nitel for 5 years at 20%, Mzuzu by Technobrain at 15% (markets only), Zomba by Nitel at 3% (markets only), and that changes to back-end data needed the vendor.

The IGC study says the cities have no comprehensive IT strategy and adopted piecemeal systems, and that there was no overarching national push to adopt them; the document is dated August 2023 and gives no date for this finding beyond the research period.
The IGC study says Mzuzu's earlier REMOP property-rates system, introduced in 2013, was provided by donors under a donor-funded programme.

facts.fact: UNDP Malawi reports that Mwanza District Council uses LORMIS to issue electronic tickets for market fees, vehicle parking and border entry fees and has a business registration component; the story says the system tracks who has paid and who has not, but does not describe a register of payers with bills against them.

UNDP Malawi describes LORMIS as a system built and run by the Mwanza District Council's own systems analyst, working on an Android application and a second platform, with supervisors at the council office tracing transactions; it states no reporting to a national system.
UNDP Malawi states that Mwanza is using all components of LORMIS; its developer hopes more districts will adopt it, and no other council or total of councils is given.
UNDP Malawi states that Mwanza adopted LORMIS with the support of the United Nations Development Programme; the developer is the council's own systems analyst and no ministry owner is named.

facts.fact: Lilongwe City Council's policy statement says it will deploy a computerized property information management system for billing and collection of property rates, under a land-based revenue modernization activity covering four cities of Malawi; it is a plan, not a live system.

Lilongwe City Council's policy statement says the United States has agreed to provide US$24 million in grant funding under the Millennium Challenge second compact to finance the land-based revenue modernization activity in four cities, including digital mapping, automated property records and a computerized billing system.
